To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the best NERC system for DeReKo is the CRF-based system (IIi) the best model for this system is the model learnt on the training data consisting of the 10% smallest DeReKo subcorpora (iii) the best model is the model that is trained on the training data that is most similar to the evaluation data and (iv) the best model outperforms all other models on the evaluation data.

(i) a system that is trained on a representative sample performs best when applied to the target corpus and that (ii) a system that has been trained on the entire target corpus performs worse than the system that has been evaluated on a representative sample.

(1) a simple rule-based approach performs best on DeReKo; (2) the best performing system for DeReKo is the one which is based on a combination of a rule-based approach and a statistical approach; and (3) the best performing model is a combination of two models, one based on a statistical approach and one based on a rule-based approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: Which of the three different NERC system architectures performs best when trained on DeReKo?
the following questions: How can we train and evaluate NERC systems on a large unbalanced corpus?
the following questions: How do different NERC systems compare on DeReKo?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single NERC system or model which performs best on all three evaluation data sets.
the best performing NERC system on the representative sample of DeREKO is CRFsuite (Okazaki, 2007).

the best performing NERC system on our sample data is the German version of the CoNLL 2003 shared task system (Sünderhauf, 2011), which is based on a maximum entropy model and which is trained on a combination of the CoNELL 2002 and 2003 training data, the German Treebank 2.0 and the German Wikipedia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have successfully demonstrated that a state-of-the-art NERC system can be trained on a very large and unbalanced corpus, and we have also shown that it can achieve high performance on the evaluation data.
we show how to use the NERC system that is optimal for the task at hand, i.e. named entity tagging a very large corpus.
the system that has been trained on the most diverse training data and evaluated on the most diverse evaluation data performs best on the most diverse test data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a simple and widely available NERC system (the Stanford NERC system, based on the CRF algorithm) is the most suitable one for DeReKo.
a simple NERC model based on conditional random fields (CRFs) and a small set of features performs best on the evaluation sample.
a NERC system that is trained and evaluated on DeReKo's representative sample performs best when applied to tagging the entire corpus.
